items.body: The title gives it away. ]ex(s)it(u)[ is a “concept album.” The cover photograph might initially suggest a bucolic collection of field recordings, but Leonardo Barbierato has other ideas. Birdsong is indeed one of the first sounds we hear, accompanied by delicate guitar plucking and live processing. From the outset, the surrounding environment enters into the performance alongside instrumental gestures, electronics and the acoustic properties of each location. Each of the seven Patchwork pieces functions as an individual study within a larger trajectory. Their subtitles — “margine” [margin], “l’ora di punta” [peak hour], “la mania del controllo” [control freakery], “frammenti di frizione eco-tonale” [fragments of ecotonal friction], “infestazione” [infestation], “condizionamento” [conditioning] and “hauntology” — provide a loose conceptual map. As Barbierato explains in the accompanying interview, the recordings grew out of five years of site-specific performances, with the characteristics of each location feeding directly into the music. The album only came into focus retrospectively, when excerpts from those performances were edited into a coherent sequence. Throughout ]ex(s)it(u)[, electronics, acoustic gestures and environmental recordings continually interact, their respective roles shifting from one piece to the next. Barbierato calls this condition “eco-tonality”, describing the intertwining of ecosystemic and performative sounds and the fluid identities that result. “l’ora di punta” allows guitar melodies to emerge from and disappear back into circuitry; “la mania del controllo” frustrates attempts to impose stable order through heightened sound levels; “frammenti di frizione eco-tonale” places different sonic ecologies within a rarefied environment; while the textures of “infestazione” proliferate across the acoustic field. The extended “condizionamento” reintroduces birdsong, which grows increasingly synthetic before giving way to a slow accumulation of density and abrasion and a roughening of texture. “hauntology” turns towards the residue left by sound, retrieving voices that seem to belong to another timeframe. For all the variety of its source material, ]ex(s)it(u)[ holds together remarkably well. Guitar, electronics, birds, voices, resonance and the acoustics of individual sites move in and out of focus across the seven pieces. Barbierato’s “eco-tonality” ultimately describes something quite practical here: a way of performing in which the sounds already present in a place can alter the direction of the music as it happens. photo by Devadatta “Sk!” Valmiki, 2025 To help us piece things together, we reached out directly to Leonardo Barbierato. Throughout ]ex(s)it(u)[, the seven Patchwork pieces seem to form a conceptual progression: from “margine”, where different sonic worlds first come into contact, through “l’ora di punta”, “la mania del controllo”, “frammenti di frizione eco-tonale”, “infestazione” and “condizionamento”, before arriving at “hauntology”, where what remains is no longer the sound itself but its residue in memory. Were these seven pieces conceived as successive stages of a single compositional journey, or did that overarching narrative emerge only retrospectively? At what point did you realise they belonged together as one work rather than as independent electroacoustic studies? The seven pieces belong to a single performative and compositional process that unfolded over the course of five years. At the beginning, I was interested in exploring the ecosystems in which I performed through improvisation. This led me to develop a series of site-specific performances entitled [in situ], where the aim was to engage with the place to the point that it could actively shape the performance itself, avoiding to treat the place as a backdrop. Initially, I had no intention of releasing this material. In a sense, doing so seemed to contradict the very idea of site-specificity on which [in situ] was based. Those performances were conceived as experiences in which listening was inseparable from the materiality of the place: its light, its physical presence, and the network of relationships and perceptions that define a particular environment. However, when I listened back to the recordings, I realised that publishing selected excerpts could open up another layer of meaning. I became interested both in the sonic interactions that had emerged during the performances and in the idea that these recordings would be heard in places completely different from those in which they were created. I was curious about how this displacement might reshape the listening experience. So, to answer your question more directly: although all seven pieces originate from the same artistic process, the overall narrative of ]ex(s)it(u)[ only emerged retrospectively, during the editing and listening phase. It was then that I recognised the trajectory connecting the excerpts, a trajectory that, to some extent, also follows the chronology of the original performances. Your background combines jazz improvisation with artistic research in ecology, and your current doctoral work explores the relationship between improvisation and cultural and environmental ecology. Listening to ]ex(s)it(u)[, I was struck by how the field recordings — birdsong, environmental ambiences and site-specific sounds — never function simply as documentary material. They seem to interact with instrumental and electronic sounds until their identities become almost indistinguishable. How do you approach this dialogue between recorded environments and composed material? Are you trying to preserve the identity of a place, or are you more interested in allowing those places to be transformed through the compositional process? While working on my PhD at the Conservatory of Rome, which I recently completed, I became increasingly aware of how environmental sounds and what we conventionally call “musical” sounds gradually overlapped and entered into dialogue. Interestingly, this was also something noticed by people attending the performances. In my research, I describe this quality as eco-tonality: a condition in which ecosystemic and performative elements become intertwined. In most of the pieces on ]ex(s)it(u)[, the environmental sounds are not field recordings added afterwards. They are the actual sounds that were present during the performances and were processed in real time through an electroacoustic setup. Only in a couple of pieces (“frammenti di frizione eco-tonale” and “hauntology”) I used dedicated field recordings, which were nevertheless recorded in the same environments where the performances took place. My intention was to place all these elements into dialogue without establishing a clear hierarchy between them. Ultimately, the project has both an ecological and a political dimension. It seeks to encourage a more attentive mode of listening and a deeper engagement with the ecosystems we inhabit. I believe that composition can function as a device that subtly transforms the way we perceive and experience the places we live in. In that sense, I am less interested in preserving the “identity” of a place than in exploring its transformative potential through listening. One of the most remarkable aspects of the album is its treatment of listening itself. By the time “condizionamento” unfolds, the music seems to have subtly altered the listener’s expectations: instead of following individual events, one begins listening to relationships, resonances and the spaces between sounds. Was this gradual transformation of perception something you consciously composed? More broadly, do you think of ]ex(s)it(u)[ as a work that conditions the listener’s way of hearing as much as it presents a sequence of sounds? I’m really pleased to read your observation, because it touches on something that was central to the project. Yes, the gradual transformation of perception you describe is something I consciously sought during the performances over the years, and later tried to recreate through the selection, editing and sequencing of the material that became ]ex(s)it(u)[. As I mentioned earlier, the album aims to influence the way we listen. This intention is rooted in the belief that aesthetics, ethics and politics are deeply interconnected. I believe that changing the way we listen can also open up different ways of thinking, relating to others and inhabiting the environments around us. However, I don’t think there is a “correct” way of listening or a predetermined ethical outcome. What interests me is the possibility that listening differently may enable each person to inhabit and relate to the world in their own way, according to their experiences, memories and ways of making sense of them. In times of social and ecological crisis, I believe that the possibility of listening and acting differently can become particularly meaningful. For me, this is where the political dimension of the work lies: in creating the conditions for a different mode of attention. Whether that change lasts for a few minutes or extends beyond the listening experience is, of course, something each listener will discover in their own way. The album artwork quietly maps the Patchwork pieces onto a series of specific locations — from Morra’s Studio in Asti to the Parco Nazionale della Maremma, the Mattatoio di Testaccio and other sites — suggesting that geography itself forms part of the composition. Combined with the recurring use of field recordings, this gives the impression that ]ex(s)it(u)[ is almost a cartography of listening rather than simply an electroacoustic album. How important was the notion of site in shaping the project? Do you see these places as sources of sound, as collaborators in the creative process, or as traces that continue to resonate long after the recordings themselves have been transformed? At the beginning of the project, I spent a long time questioning what it means to act in a site-specific way and, more fundamentally, what a place actually is. Each piece on ]ex(s)it(u)[ is an excerpt from a specific performance of [in situ], connected to a specific location. The geography of these places is mapped in the artwork, allowing the listener to associate each track with its original context while listening. I really enjoy the expression “cartography of listening” that you used, as it captures an important aspect of the project. Throughout this process, I always tried to avoid treating places as soundscapes from which to extract material to manipulate freely. When I used field recordings, they emerged from encounters with the ecosystems themselves: for example, through conversations and interviews with the communities I encountered in different locations, who often pointed me towards sounds, events or relationships that were meaningful to them. In most cases, however, these sounds emerged directly during the performances: the movements of participants, objects being touched or activated, birdsong, cicadas, wind, my playing and all the other sonic events that became part of the situation. This is central to my understanding of site-specific practice: a place is an entanglement of personal, human and other-than-human stories, relationships and forms of agency that actively shape the compositional and performative process. For me, a place is a kind of patchwork, where each patch (each element that contributes to its identity) follows its own trajectory and interacts with others, sometimes in harmony, sometimes in conflict, and sometimes with indifference. Through this work, I try to make these relationships perceptible on a sonic level and to reflect on them actively. In this sense, the place collaborates with and co-produces ]ex(s)it(u)[. It remains beyond the production of the work itself, continuing to resonate and transform through each new listening experience. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.excerpt: Poladroïd packs eight lean, muscular tracks with throbbing bass, fat drum-machine punch and just enough EBM grit to keep the whole thing moving. items.body: Poladroïd packs eight lean, muscular tracks with throbbing bass, fat drum-machine punch and just enough EBM grit to keep the whole thing moving. Lean, mean and mechanical Poladroïd drops this lean eight-tracker of electro industriana, fusing lino-friendly aesthetics with European body-music gloss and a distinctly modern tech-funk sensibility. The moods are taut and tensile, the bottom end throbbing in post-Moroder blasts while the drums come in big and fat, all Roger Linn punch and TR-909 muscle. The result is an album that understands restraint but never sounds restrained. “Norilsk” opens proceedings with clean-air funk and a diabolically wiry synth topline that cascades like digital waterfalls. Warm pads gradually move into the frame, adding color and perspective as the track develops into a convincing soul-and-machine coalescence. “Lyuberi” follows with straight-up EBM propulsion, its hard pulse surrounded by huge string synths that give the track a cinematic glow without softening its physical impact. “Leningrad” reveals Mr Droid as someone not inclined to follow the routines of the pack, bending familiar electro and industrial grammar into something more individual and elusive. “Sochi” twists and turns through helter-skelter synth melodies, constantly changing direction while maintaining its​ muscular rhythmic center. We are now only halfway through as Roentgenizdat—The Soviet-era practice of copying banned Western and émigré music onto discarded X-ray film to evade state censorship—begins its closing moments “Girls From Omsk” digs deepest into the groove, riding a simple, infectious refrain that becomes increasingly impossible to shake. “White Boy Funk” steps forward on a clipped rhythm and wiry bassline, its fogged-out strings creating a sense of pressure and anticipation. “Doomer” brings the industrial vocal miasma, gruff and ominous, with proto-paranoia steadily gathering behind the beat. Closer “Escape To Tbilisi” finally lets everything off the leash: a stomping, skewed belter that sends the album out at full mechanical tilt. Roentgenizdat is available on Roulette Rekordz. items.body: Review by ZowieZiggy — Mark one in concert! A a very rare document. I discovered oit recently TKX to YouTube. And since I am a HUGE Purple fan (since December 1970...), I listened to it and decided to post a reviw about this concert. Purple played at Inglewood as guest for Cream!The audio is quiete good I must say. And what we'll get here is a kaleidoscope of all Mark I albums.The good point (at least in IMHHO) is that the band is not going to improvise too much on such numbers as "Mandrake Roots" as well as "Wring that Neck". Two numbers from their own compositions that will be over extended during the Mark II era. Up to almost half an hour!So, here they will be played in a "classic" way, and that's very fine.The covers are very ell rendered and sooooo pleasant as well: "Help!" is gorgeous. And i have to admit that Rod's vocals work perfectly here. His tone of voice is pretty adequate I must say. and I'm gnerally not very laudatory about it to say the least. So, when it is good, one has to ackowledge, right?My fave of all is "River Deep, Mountain High". almost 10 minutes starting with the theme from "2001, A Space Odissey" and there after, rocking quite well.Even if there won't be many readers about this live album, it gives a pretty good feeling about what were the Mark I concert. And therefore my interest.The band sounds very united and happy to play together. But in the background, things might have been different, hence the sacking of Rod & Nick a year later. Leading to the most fabulous (IMHO) period of Purple. Namely Mark II.This live set ends with their biggest hit, nameley "Hey Joe" that will rank in the US Bilboard.All in all, this is a pretty good record. I rate it with 4****.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — The Roaring Waves by Hackett & Rothery sees 2 prog rock guitar legends coming together to create a very enjoyable if slightly tedious instrumental album. No one can take away the impact Steve Hackett & Steve Rothery have on the progressive rock world, with early Genesis & Marillion being a massive influence on the entire modern prog scene since the 70s & 80s, and their monumental playing is always an ace card. But while they bring such talent to these bands, they are the type of guitarists who contribute to a group more than themselves as solo instrumentalists. But the noticeable styles between the 2 are noticeable and they do compliment each other well. The tracks are very well composed and performed, but there isn't too much meat on the bone. It is overall very well mixed too. I'd give this a high 6 to low 7 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is The Roaring Waves.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 987"The Roaring Waves" is a collaborative album by two influential names in the European prog scene, Steve Hackett and Steve Rothery. As we know, Hackett was the main guitarist of Genesis and Rothery is the guitarist of Marillion. As we also know, Marillion was the band most close to Genesis of all British prog bands that appeared in the 80's. So, we can say that Rothery is, somehow, the heir of Hackett on guitars. So, we can not be surprised by this collaborative effort.Although the initial idea emerged around 2015, "The Roaring Waves" took nearly a decade to be written and recorded. The sessions were split between the Racket Club (Marillion's studio) and the home studios of both musicians. The strong connection between both solidified on stage when Rothery joined Hackett at the Royal Albert Hall in 2024 to play "Fly On A Windshield", one of the most famous tracks of the album "The Lamb Lies Down On Broadway" by Genesis.So, "The Roaring Waves" is the first instrumental collaborative project between two of the most iconic guitarists in progressive rock. The album is a profoundly cinematic, atmospheric and a melodic work, entirely inspired by the power, mysteries and nuances of the sea, beautifully paced conversation between two master guitarists. Instead of a flashy "speed trial" or shred-fest competition, the album prioritizes compositional patience, atmospheric depth, and melodic trade-offs. Hackett's angular, classical-tinged and experimental approach, merges seamlessly with Rothery's emotional soaring sustain. Having decided to completely forgo vocals and lyrics, the album gives the listener a true complete imaginative freedom through textures that blend progressive rock, classical music, ambient and electronic textures.The line up on "The Roaring Waves" is Steve Hackett (guitar and harmonica) and Steve Rothery (guitar, bass guitar and keyboards). "The Roaring Waves" also had the participation of Riccardo Romano (keyboards and bass guitar), Daniele Pomo and Leon Parr (drums)."The Storm" is the dramatic opening of the album. It begins by placing the listener in the midst of a storm, with the guitars intertwining to create the tension and force of a storm at sea. This is a beautiful, wild and cinematic piece that delights the listener, a track that serves more as an introduction to the album than in a particularly loud announcement. "Sandsend" is a more restful and contemplative track, where the tension eases, evoking a sense of isolation, a cool beauty and serene atmospheres. It veers a measured rhythm, toward elegant and melancholic atmospheres reminiscent of Pink Floyd, letting the guitars literally sing in unison. At under five minutes, the track is correspondingly compact. "Red Dragon" is the shortest track on the album where Hackett introduces the sitar guitar to give the composition a mystical and an oriental sound. It brings a touch of world music to the otherwise rather watertight soundscape with folkloric influences, bagpipes and sitar sounds. This is a more playful and less polished piece than its predecessors. The title track "The Roaring Waves" is probably the most compelling moment on the album. It begins with a beautiful flourish of classical guitar by Hackett. It's one of the album's highlights, the real swell. Slowly, the swelling dynamics, guitars giving each other space, and precisely that blend of melancholy and pathos for both Steves, a real classic prog moment. "K-129" is one of the most experimental and intriguing tracks on the album. Electronic soundscapes and dark guitars create a very own feeling. Once again, this rhythmic framework is layered over the two guitarists in a largely improvisational style. It stands out paying homage to the "Kosmische Musik" and the Berlin School of the 70's. It reminds me of "Gento", by Bisocope of last year, the project of Rothery and Thorsten Quaeschning of Tangerine Dream. For me, it's one of the strongest tracks on the album. "The Black Sea", described by the authors as a dark adventure, was chosen as the lead single of the album. It's one of the album's great melancholic beauties. Rothery's warm guitar meets Hackett's finely crafted timbres. This is precisely where it becomes clear why this collaboration makes any sense at all. "Pacific Coast Highway" departs from the gray and icy atmosphere of the previous tracks, an unexpected track. Here, the music gains rhythm and movement with Hackett playing harmonica and slide guitar, evoking a high-speed car trip along the sunny California coast. It's a lighthearted, road-movie-esque jam with plenty of vocals at the end of it.Conclusion: "The Roaring Waves" is a dialogue between two musicians who respect and listen to each other, and who have acquired the wisdom of guitarists who have nothing left to prove. It's, therefore, a mature, profound and extremely refined work. "The Roaring Waves" remains above all an album on which two guitarists thankfully dedicate themselves not to themselves, but to the respective piece and its shared concept. Hackett and Rothery harmonize superbly with each other, instead of getting lost in an endless competition for the more spectacular solo. Compared with the album "GTR" of Hackettt and Howe, this is a much better work. I know, those were the 80's. But I don't know if it's an excuse.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

It's a semi fullyinstrumental album, with the only spoken sections being some indigenous like chants on the secondtrack "Visi�n planetaria de los tiempos", which seem to be in a native American language, I'd say itmost likely is Mapudungun, however, these chants and lyrics have no subtitles available on thedescription of the track (at least on platforms such as Spotify), and the singer seems to beuncredited, ladies and gentlemen this is the mystery I told you about! What do these lyrics meanexactly, and who sang them? It's captivating how a detail so simple can imply so many things!Musically wise, the music delivers an interesting experience which mixes krautrock with psychedelicrock and some elements of Zeuhl. Speaking of Zeuhl, it seems to be one of the main genres the bandlooks up to, as their publicly available playlist is dominated by bands such as Magma and Weidorje,as well as kasutrock acts like Popol Vuh and Amon D��l II, interestingly enough, we find some ratherodd influences that stand out in their playlist, like the extreme doom metal band Sunnata. Beinghighly influenced by classic experimental genres characterized by their use of symphonicinstrumentation, tape effects, spiritual topics and repetitiveness, "Impermanencia" is full ofsynthetizers, tape loops, repetitions of bass lines and riffs and a very hypotonic, spiral like windof textures and noises, all contributing to the creation of pieces which feel less like music andmore akin to a state of trance and meditation, albeit a very chaotic one. Each composition feelsvery much like the previous one, with little variation in the state it indices on the listener, thisoverall calmer and more meditative approach to music, will appeal to those invested in ambient andkraut, but won't satisfy those who prefer Zeuhl or more expressive, grandiose symphonic rock. The album has a lot of influences, although most can't be felt, but when it shows the signs, itsounds great! I'd like to point out that I was fairly dissapointed, as I was promised a magnum opus,a masterclass for the genre and most of the times, the record feels like an experiment halfway doneor a very relaxing jamming session.The musicianship is good enough, you can feel that each instrument was recorded separately and thenpieced together with the others, they are talented players but you can't really feel much chemistrybetween the parts that make the music, if you add this to what I previously stated, you get the fullpicture : this record is much more like something "Stars of the lid" would do if they went a littlemore experimental and not something that comes out of the chaotic mess of Zeuhl or the mathematicsof krautrock.My biggest issue with this record is the production, which is straight up unbearable...this recordsounds muddy, grainy, blurry and inconsistent, because yes, some tracks have good production and theother an awful one, and the difference is so noticeable it makes it uncomfortable to listen to. Thedrums can't even be heard most of the time, a record so inspired by krautrock should have a veryclear rhythmic direction and presence, which can't be heard through at least half of the record.I give it 2 stars because it's an interesting record to dig into and because of how hypnotic anduseful for meditation it is, but musically itself, I don't really see much to highlight...it'salmost as if it were an experiment that was never properly finished, this is sad because thisproject had so much potential.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Over its near-20 years of existence, Utah's Rylee McDonald has seen his high school musical project turn into a kind of family affair, now adding his partner and wife and their two children to the mix. Still, the Rush- and Led Zeppelin-inspired artist has emerged as his own musical force.1. "In A Lone and Dreary World" (19:03) a djenty low end does not deter this prog extravaganza from taking us on a journey that reminds me of the music of 21st Century projects like LIFESIGNS and NUMEN and even COSMOGRAF and DAVE BRONS . . . (if a little metal edge were applied). Though I am not a fan of this kind of "plastic" drum sound, I very much appreciate the skills and creativity of the performance on the batterie exhibited here by Mike Lofgreen (though it is also mixed into the soundscape as a kind of anomaly of isolated individually-distinguished sterility; that is, the rest of the sounds are given those standard effects we now associate automatically with prog, i.e. reverbs, distortions, gates, sustains, compressions, etc.) Oh! really love the voice of Kristen McDonald. The collective sound of the band's vocal palette reminds me of short-lived band from Naughties, THE REASONING as well as second- and third- album PURE REASON REVOLUTION (2009's Amor Vincit Omnia and 2010's Hammer and Anvil). Paired up with those syncopated djenty guitar chords and we have quite a cool sound and mix. Then you have to take into consideration the common human plight being expressed in the song lyrics: dissatisfaction and distrust of all we've been raised to believe and value, all we've been told--including that coming from parents and family--learning to listen to and trust one's own inner voice and inner truths and beliefs--the awakening to the power of a spiritual perspective (perhaps even a Christian rebirth): "No enemies" and "saved and sound." Though the length taken to deliver the message/story is a bit over-protracted, it is effective and well-rendered with little or no fluff and appropriate nuance and theatrics. Nice work. (36.5/40) 2. "Faiths Window" (5:20) with industrial horn humming in the background a dirty-distorted electric guitar's two-chord strum repeats itself, occasionally moving between subtly different chords as Rylee McDonald sing/talks over the top, turning into singing as the rest of the band's sound cascades into the mix. It's heavy but it's symphonic with the layers of instruments easy to distinguish from each other. In the fourth minute the lyrics are delivered through growl-screams before the McDonald family choir takes over. A metal instrumental passage takes over with searing electric guitar, etc. but then Kristen emerges as the lead vocalist, taking us to the song's (rather sudden) end. (8.875/10)3. "Patience" (4:53) a normal rock sound palette over which Rylee's single male voice leads the way gradually turns heavy metal with the chorus, playing out as such into the final fadeout of electronic keyboards. A solid song but there is nothing very new or innovative here. (8.75/10)4. "Past Life Parable" (5:03) more solid heavy prog steering toward the more sophisticated hair band sounds and music of the 1970s and 1980s, the big difference here is the use of djenty guitar chords and some more-modern sounds as well as an admirable level of sophistication in the construct/composition. (8.875/10)5. "Gravity I" (2:35) nice Spanish acoustic guitar play surrounded by proggy drum 'n' bass and textural synth washes and other keyboard and, eventually, electric guitar effects. Impressive drum play toward the end--just before the transition/bridge to "Gravity II." (4.625/5) 6. "Gravity II" (4:49) bleeding over from the previous "introductory" song, Rylee's voice in the lead position is backed/doubled by Kristen. Nice use of organ bass pedals and harpsichord sound in the third minute, but then we are quickly back into the metal, even djenty music long before the minute's end. I really like the guitar djent-play in this section (as well as the more subdued vocal performance), but then we shift back into hyperdrive with the machine gun bass pedal play for a few bars before cutting out for a near-a cappella passage, but then we nearly as quickly and suddenly find ourselves back in the fray of machine gun beats and rapid-fire beat-down low end guitar chords. Still, I like and respect it overall. (9/10)7. "Animals" (5:34) Rylee's single male voice is singing while only accompanied by lone acoustic guitar picking. After one time through a round of the verse and chorus the keys, bass pedals, and stark drum play join in the now split (R & L) two-acoustic guitar picking foundation. I wish I could pick out who Rylee's voice reminds me of: it's definitely one of STYX's lead vocalists: either Tommy Shaw or Dennis DeYoung. The McDonald family choir is cited for this song but their role is, sadly, rather quiet, minor. Still, this is a pretty cool song--one that only lacks for seriously brainworm melodies. (9.125/10) Total Time 47:17The McDonald family's sound and style cannot help but be compared to the bands mentioned above--especially THE REASONING and early PURE REASON REVOLUTION but also bands like RUSH, STYX, INTROITUS and MEER. From its Led Zeppelin inspiration and Rush fueling and modeling, the band seems to have come into its own: into something that sounds like . . . but is really their own thing--which is really nice.A-/five stars; though this kind of Classic Rock and sophisticated 80s Metal blend of prog is not really among my high preferences, I do appreciate the creative and complex song structures built here as well as the wonderful vocal work rendered by the collective members of the McDonald family (really, Rylee and Kristen).

items.body: Review by Neuroprog — Octobre is one of the first progressive rock albums from Quebec, released in 1973. The wonderful compositions on this album allow Pierre Flynn to showcase his full talent. He is truly one of Quebec's finest singers, a real hidden gem. Overall, the songs are built around powerful and catchy riffs. This is therefore not the most progressive album out there: it does not particularly seek to push musical boundaries or necessarily build toward epic moments. It is instead one of the great Quebec rock albums, with clear influences from the progressive rock movement of the time. It was only after this album that the band would go on to develop and complicate its compositions further. It is unfortunate that this excellent album and band are not nearly as well known as Harmonium, Robert Charlebois, Beau Dommage, Offenbach, Paul Pich�, and others.More specifically, the album features a lot of changes in rhythm despite containing only eight tracks and running for less than 30 minutes. We go from songs like Si on partait, a more straightforward rock song with a frantic pace, to much more nuanced and slower pieces featuring melancholic lyrics sung beautifully by Pierre Flynn. Flynn also shines on several tracks with his expressive organ and piano solos.To fully appreciate this album, it is essential to understand French, and especially "joual", as well as the Quebec specific references of the period. Dans ma ville is a perfect example of a song built around two completely different tempos. You can feel the musical crescendo throughout the verses before everything comes back down for a gentle chorus, conveying the feelings of anger and nostalgia that run through the song. This combination of emotion and rhythm is present throughout the album, reinforcing the power of Flynn's vocals.The closing track, La maudite machine, is an anthem in which the importance of the lyrics takes precedence over the melody. Strangely enough, it is the best-known song on the album, although it is not necessarily the most musically interesting one.4/5

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — One of Radiohead's founding guitarists (and still member) Ed O'Brien releases his second studio album as a solo artist. I don't know any of the guest musician/collaborators but you can bet that Ed had his pick of the cr'me de la cr'me!1. "Incantations" (7:41) a single repeating acoustic guitar arpeggio provides the bed for 1:45 of Ed's folk singing. It honestly sounds like something from an early Roy Harper album. Other instruments, hand percussives and electronics, join in to move the music into territory previously traveled by the likes of DONOVAN and BJ'RK. Floating background vocals sound like Bj'rk's Inuit Choir on the Vespero tours. At 5:40 the percussionist(s) are joined by drums, electric bass, electric guitars, and keyboard atmospherics--which play out until slowly being faded out while Dave Okumu's bass and Ed's reverberating guitar notes continue to the song's end. Cool song! (13.875/15)2. "Blue Morpho" (6:18) another really cool atmospheric sonosphere created by guitars, wordless vocals, bass, synth washes, and, this time, full symphony strings. It's quite lovely--even moving: chords and multiple melody lines floating, flowing, shifting, morphing, and melding into one gorgeous textural feast. And the whole time I'm feel quite a little debt owed (or homage given) to George Martin and The Beatles. (Think of songs like "Blackbird" and "I Am the Walrus" as well as albums like Magical Mystery Tour.) Brilliant and beautiful! (9.75/10)3. "Sweet Spot" (4:10) double lines of picked acoustic guitar chords woven into one though coming from both sides of the stage starts out this beautiful, atmospheric and kind of eerie (like GRAVENHURST) music over/within which Ed sings both lead and backing vocals. I like the way the orchestra strings slowly move to the fore as Ed's lead voice sinks into the instrumental mix. Eventually, the strings (and, I'll assume, keyboard electronics) end up alone, finishing the song after everybody/everything else has left. Not as memorable as the previous songs but rewarded for the creative sound and structural tactics. (9/10)4. "Teachers" (5:18) a funky bass 'n' drum pattern is surrounded and permeated by eerie atmospherics. Ed's heavily-treated ghost-voice enters toward the end of the first minute, singing in a pleasant monotone for a minute or so but then it leaves, whereupon the bass, drums, guitars, and synths all seem to spread out into loose, adventurous swaths away from but still anchored in the main theme. The final minute sees the vocal choir sing, "open wide" before the instruments all stop or fade away, leaving only weird electronic noises to close out the song. (8.875/10)5. "Solfeggio" (2:36) guitar/electronic harpsichord chord perpetuated with sustain and arpeggiation open this before more layers of voice-originating atmospherics enter and steer the with an eerie yet unthreatening kind of melody line, repeated over and over before signing off with a final lower-register three-note sequence, all the while the glitchy electronica effects are increasingly present, even rising to a driver's position, like something from a SyFy Continuum soundtrack experience (think Au4's "Everyone Is Everyone [and Everything Is Everything]"). More genius song/sound making. (4.4375/5)6. "Thin Places" (2:19) flute, wordless voice, synthetics all woven together to create a kind of dream-like out-of-body astral travel experience. (4.4375/5)7. "Obrigado" (9:53) a very cool, almost jazz-lite rhythm track over/within which Ed & Co. deliver some pretty awesome atmospherics (as well as vocals). The reverse-delay guitar effects for Ed's guitar solo in the seventh and eighth minutes are only surpassed by the dreamy psychedelic soundscape floating and morphing beneath it (and, later, by the amazing wordless vocal tracks raging in the background--which I think one must attribute to Clare Torey-inspired Awsa Berstrom). Ed's ultra-cool voice reminds me of both George Harrison, Gadi Caplan, Donovan, and Harry Nilsson as well as, you know, Radiohead. Really a cool, amazing, and powerful song. A pleasure to listen to every single time I do. (19.5/20)Total Time 38:15It's weird how much/how often I hear core/key Radiohead sounds in Ed's music here. This leads me to feel strongly how important and integral he was/is to the Radiohead sound--to their music.A/five stars; a brilliant display of creative/innovative sound and song crafting that stands out as a masterpiece of extrapolated future music (as if Ed's projecting himself into the 22nd Century or beyond--or even another dimension). A modern musical masterpiece. Highly recommended. One of the best albums I've heard from 2026.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Although the Trans-Siberian Orchestra project was already well underway following the success of 1996's "Christmas Eve & Other Stories", Jon Oliva and Savatage still had a lot to offer as a band. Thus, in 1997, the American band released their tenth album, "The Wake of Magellan". A conceptual rock opera inspired by the reflections of an elderly and solitary former sailor, H�ctor Del-Fuego Magellan -a fictional character who claims to be a descendant of the famous Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan- whose story is intertwined with various contemporary events (the 1996 murder of Irish journalist Veronica Guerin for her investigations into drug trafficking, and the stowaways on the freighter Maersk Dubai, whose dramatic fate also unfolded that year).The sound of the sea in the instrumental and cinematic "The Ocean" and the festive, Broadway-esque track "Welcome" set the stage for H�ctor to begin a bitter retrospective on his life, ranging from the despondency reflected in dramatic power ballads like "Turns to Me" or "Morning Sun"-crowned by Al Pitrelli's superb and forceful guitar solos- to the seething helplessness and the decision to end his life out at sea, channeled through corrosive, heavy riffs in the '80s-style "Another Way" or the psychotic "Blackjack Guillotine" and "Paragons of Innocence," tracks that draw on influences spanning a wide spectrum from hard rock to metal.The atmosphere of mounting tension that pervades the album reaches its highest peaks in the progressive track "The Wake of Magellan" -an epic that stands as the album's crowning jewel, built upon the wall of sound created by Johnny Lee Middleton on bass, Jeff Plate on drums, and Oliva on piano, culminating in spirited polyphonic harmonies- and in the stormy instrumental "The Storm," featuring another great solo by Pitrelli. And it is only in the theatrical and epic "The Hourglass" that the conflicted character finally finds solace in redemption and a purpose for his life."The Wake of Magellan" is not only an ambitious rock opera but also one of Savatage's most conceptually rich works.Very good.3.5/4 stars

items.body: Review by higgins — There are debuts that sound like debuts, with that mixture of timidity and overreach so typical of someone still searching for their place, and there are debuts that arrive already carrying the astonishing confidence of people who've been playing together for half a lifetime without anyone quite noticing. Datura Lodge decidedly belongs to this second lineage. And it's no coincidence: Nicky B and W. have known each other and played together since their teens, something that comes through in every breath of this self-titled album, a chemistry that can't be improvised or bought in any studio, however good it may be.I listened to this record thanks to a promo copy the label was kind enough to send me, and I'm deeply grateful for it, because Datura Lodge is one of those works you'd rather have stumbled upon yourself, tripping over it in a record shop, and yet here we are, with the good fortune of having had it in hand ahead of time.The New Jersey duo doesn't hide its sources, nor should it. There's a melodic streak that leads straight back to Genesis, especially in those moments when the vocal reaches for the hook without giving up harmonic complexity. And there's something else too, something of our own era: that way of organizing the chaos, of metering out the tension and releasing it at exactly the right moment, which inevitably brings to mind a more restrained Steven Wilson, or his band Porcupine Tree on the days it decides to smile.Tracks like "Stone" or "Can" show that technique serves emotion rather than the other way around, with an instrumental display (Adam Holzman is in there on keys, contributing a great deal) that never tips into gratuitous showmanship. But it's in the fragility of "Hole" or the almost uncomfortable honesty of "Them" where Datura Lodge reveals its true nature: an album that knows how to laugh at itself while talking about rootlessness, generational disillusionment, and the strange task of staying human amid a full digital shipwreck.Datura Lodge doesn't reinvent progressive rock, but it inhabits it with a naturalness and a joy of playing that are sorely missed in so many current releases, more concerned with orthodoxy than with life.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The affirmation often has a psychological value that operates at an unconscious level; it begins from the outside and ends up taking hold internally. The Yes Album was a new beginning for many reasons: the first to feature Steve Howe, the first in which the compositions of Anderson, Chris Squire, and soon Howe would acquire that classic status and the first where rock, jazz, and a distinctive balance between acoustic and electric elements would find their signature style and a home within the progressive universe.There are many classic Yes lineups, and although the subsequent era might be considered the "classic of classics," the 1971 period is already worthy of that title. Gathering at Langley Farm, they recorded a handful of songs that would become enduring favorites, not only for that lineup but for those that followed, and have been performed live ever since.I'm a fan of the Peter Banks era, but Steve Howe, while retaining that affinity for rock 'n' roll, jazz, and classical music, brought a rhythm, a groove, and a fingering style, along with a cosmic dimension, that set the band apart right from "Yours Is No Disgrace." The vocal harmonies, often bordering on a cappella, were just one of many hallmarks that emerged with this album. The band also gained a warmth and an intimacy it hadn't possessed before; tracks like "Yours Is No Disgrace" featured not only instrumental sections but also intimate moments that made for a complete experience."Clap" is the first of many acoustic tracks by Steve Howe; composed of several sections, some with a pastoral, rustic feel and others with a distinct rock-and-roll vibe, the version that made the final cut was recorded live at London's Lyceum Theatre and would forever define one of the facets of this new Yes."Starship Trooper" must be one of the first tracks that made me fall in love with the band. Jon was gradually reaching the peak of his expressive potential, conveying a genuine emotion that was reinforced by Chris Squire on bass, Bill Bruford on drums, and, son, Steve Howe on guitar (who already seemed like a full-fledged member, even though Peter Banks still appeared on the album cover!). There was a palpable sense of communion as they focused on conveying their musical vision. Tony Kaye was solid, too, though he would later be succeeded by someone with such a massive aura that it would elevate "Starship Trooper" to even greater heights. Once again, the vocal harmonies and Jon's voice stood out... and just as the emotion reached its peak, "W�rm", the third section, would kick in. Steve would start off solo, with the rest of the band gradually joining him, creating a soundscape that felt like the prelude to a space voyage and the actual liftoff. And the first of many memorable riffs with an electrifying personality.The emotional momentum didn't let up, as a powerful new surge of feeling arrived with "I've Seen All Good People", a track that is 100% Yes. The band always drew sustenance from both the technical/virtuosic side and the spiritual/emotional one; neither works without the other, and it was their combination that gave birth to their best songs and albums. The track is neatly divided into two parts: the acoustic first section, "Your Move", which carries an almost Andean feel, and the rock-driven second half, "All Good People." The two work in tandem, creating the song's magical contrast."A Venture" is an atypical and unusual track within the context of the �lbum, and a very beautiful one. It features very interesting breaks and syncopated drum and guitar work from Howe and Bruford; towards the end, Chris's bass and Tony Kaye's distinctly jazzy solo leave you wishing they would keep playing like that for even longer."Perpetual Change" is the final track, and Bill Bruford's presence is as notable as it is significant; the format, an elaborate introduction leading into a fully developed song, set a precedent for what was to come. Hints of a country feel followed by a jazz-inflected progression, along with the polyrhythms and counterpoint in the finale, exemplified the band's high level of technical proficiency. Meanwhile, the vocal interplay between Jon and Chris offered a different facet, helping to create an album that holds a unique place in history. There are many layers to consider: while the band's subsequent work was undoubtedly more complex and elaborate, and is rightly regarded as some of their best, this album possesses its own distinct value. It stands as an equally great record, not for the same reasons as the later material, but for others; after all, as we have seen, Yes is a multi-dimensional band.

items.body: “Wanga”, the newest single from Director Shaibu, lands in Afro-pop and Bongo Flava, the Swahili-language pop that has held Tanzanian radio since the late nineties. Shaibu grew up inland, in Mwanza on Lake Victoria, and trained for the screen at TaSUBa in Bagamoyo, taking director and production manager credits on Tanzanian features including Giza la Mchana and Ndoto za Kitaa. Music and Zanzibar came later… He built M-Studio at Jambiani on the east coast and released the Zanzibar EP through it in August 2024. This year came Pilau, an eleven-track album named after the spiced rice of the islands, and “Wanga” is the single he has drawn from it. Stream “Wanga” HERE and hear Pilau in full through THIS LINK   The post Daily Discovery: Director Shaibu – Wanga appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: María Dueñas partners with Gustavo Dudamel and the Simón Bolívar Symphony Orchestra of Venezuela to celebrate an artist she has long regarded as an inspiration. Jascha Heifetz’s vinyl recordings of the major works presented here—Lalo’s Symphonie espagnole and Korngold’s Violin Concerto—were ones she grew up with. She also had the opportunity to record three of the accompanying shorter works on his own 1731 ‘Heifetz, Piel’ Stradivarius. Homage to Heifetz Amazon Presto Apple Dueñas mentions that Heifetz’s soul and fire are what have shaped her own playing, and a work as striking as the Symphonie espagnole is a fitting vehicle for those qualities. The orchestra plays a part-and-parcel role in driving the extroverted, passionate spirit of the concerto, and their punchy entrance in the Allegro non troppo (track 1) commands undivided attention. Dueñas plays with plenty of verve (the opening is perhaps even more emphatic than her predecessor’s recording with William Steinberg and the RCA Victor Symphony Orchestra); there is, however, another, complementary persona that embraces lyricism and poignancy and ensures the melodiousness of Lalo’s writing is never lost. Where Dueñas and Heifetz sound most similar is perhaps in the middle register, as both lean into the strings with their bows to draw a warm, resonant presence. The Scherzando exudes playful charm as Dueñas adds a coy innocence that contrasts with the smoldering tempestuousness of the previous movement. The Bolívar players evoke a delightful levity in their neat pizzicatos and trills, upon which the soloist builds an improvisatory feel in her part. The Intermezzo (track 3) shares the vibrant character heard in the Allegro non troppo, but it is the Andante (track 4) that captures the deepest sense of pathos. The ensemble’s thick sostenuto gives Dueñas a rich background texture to work with, and her wide expressive range doesn’t disappoint: some sections express sadness at barely above a whisper, while others powerfully evoke a more tragic presence. I found Dueñas’ reading of this movement perhaps the most different from Heifetz’s, which is in some ways less outwardly intense but speaks more soulfully and profoundly to the listener. Korngold’s Violin Concerto possesses intensity, but in a manner different from the melodrama of the Lalo: its harmonic language is more adventurous and its phrasal architecture more expansive. The Moderato nobile (track 6) draws its intensity from anticipation. Dueñas shows plenty of staying power in the held notes of the high register and, together with sparkling fingerwork, reveals the composer’s lush language. The comparison with Heifetz’s recording reveals some interesting distinctions, though both capture Korngold’s cinematic essence. I found Dueñas’ tone headier and at times angular (owing partly to the bright timbre of her instrument), going hand in hand with her rhapsodic treatment of the virtuosic passages. Heifetz’s sound, meanwhile, is generally smoother yet resonant, evoking nostalgia in choice moments. The Romance (track 7) is gorgeous, capturing the tender and dreamy side of the work. Dueñas’ ability to switch to a more gossamer sound is impressive, showing that she is as much at ease with nuance as with sensation. The orchestra is highly responsive to the soloist, meeting her at every turn in its color changes and phrase contouring. The intricacies of the swashbuckling Finale (track 8) are expertly synchronized between the forces, and despite all that is going on texturally and tonally, passages are approached with clarity and ease. I was curious to hear how the switch of instrument in three of the shorter works would influence the readings. Dueñas performs Léon Roques’ arrangement of Debussy’s La plus que lente (track 10) on the Piel, and we immediately hear the violin speak in a way that recalls Heifetz’s recordings of the two concertos. The timbre is subtler yet more complex in its husky, vocal profile. Combined with her lithe phrasing and lovely soft dynamics, the result is limpid and otherworldly. Heifetz’s arrangement of La chevelure from the Chansons de Bilitis (track 11) sounds deeply intimate, with Dueñas channeling the instrument’s throatiness to create enigma and suspense. Pianist Itamar Golan proves equally receptive to the dark, almost sinister undertones. Dueñas and her collaborators give top-notch performances that do justice to a heartfelt homage. items.body: Catherine Ringer, vocalist, songwriter, and co-founder of French new wave duo Les Rita Mitsouko, has died at age 68. Her children announced her death in a statement to AFP, confirming that she died from cancer on the night of September 14, 2026. With her partner in music and life, Fred Chichin, Ringer made pop music feel large enough to accommodate almost anything: punk impatience, funk, cabaret, electronic experimentation, and the expressive possibilities of French chanson. A song could be funny, sensual, disconcerting, and profoundly sad within the same few minutes. Ringer gave each feeling its own physical presence, singing with a freedom that made conventional ideas of good taste seem rather timid. Born on October 18, 1957, in Suresnes, near Paris, she was the daughter of painter Sam Ringer, a Polish-born Jewish Holocaust survivor, and an architect mother. She left school at 15 and pursued an artistic education through theatre, music, and dance. Among the formative figures in her life was Argentine dancer and choreographer Marcia Moretto, who became her teacher and collaborator. Those years onstage helped establish the connection between movement and voice that would distinguish her work with Les Rita Mitsouko. Nostalgie’s biography documents her early performances and work with Moretto. Ringer met Chichin in 1979, beginning a partnership that would carry them from the Paris underground to international recognition. Their self-titled 1984 debut, recorded with Conny Plank, introduced a group whose appetite for experiment came with a formidable instinct for melody. As Coilhouse’s retrospective observed, Ringer’s background in avant-garde theatre remained visible in the duo’s performances and videos. Marcia Baïla became their breakthrough. Written in remembrance of Moretto following her death from cancer, it joined the exhilaration of dance to the shock of losing someone whose life had been devoted to movement. Its popularity carried that private grief into public celebration. The song offers an especially poignant way to remember Ringer now: affection, anger, and delight sharing the same space, with no easy separation between them. Directed by Philippe Gautier, the music video for Marcia Baïla gave the song an equally extravagant visual life, with costumes by Jean Paul Gaultier and Thierry Mugler. Watch the video below. The duo’s collaboration with Tony Visconti on The No Comprendo in 1986 brought Andy, C’est comme ça, and Les Histoires d’A. The album won at the 1987 Victoires de la Musique, as did Jean-Baptiste Mondino’s video for C’est comme ça. These songs remain an excellent introduction to Ringer’s range: the teasing insistence of Andy, the sharp attack of C’est comme ça, and the ease with which she could make a repeated phrase feel like an argument, an invitation, or a joke. Their creative world extended well beyond records. Jean-Luc Godard included the duo at work in his 1987 film Soigne ta droite, while collaborations brought them together with fellow musical eccentrics. Sparks joined them for Singing in the Shower, from 1988’s Marc & Robert, a meeting of artists who understood how much pleasure could be found in pop’s peculiar corners. Later, Iggy Pop appeared on My Love Is Bad, preserved alongside their other collaborations in the band’s collected catalogue. The apparent playfulness could also carry terrible knowledge. Le Petit Train addressed the deportation trains of the Holocaust, a history bound closely to her father’s survival. Its video, filmed in Bombay, placed Ringer amid exuberant dancing while the words described people being carried toward their deaths. The tension between the music’s invitation and the lyric’s meaning remains deeply unsettling. She understood how a familiar pleasure could open an audience to something painful. Chichin died from cancer in 2007, aged 53, the year Les Rita Mitsouko released Variéty. Ringer continued performing their songs while building a solo catalogue that included Ring n’ Roll in 2011 and Chroniques et fantaisies in 2017. With Plaza Francia, alongside Gotan Project’s Eduardo Makaroff and Christoph H. Müller, she explored tango on 2014’s A New Tango Song Book. Her later work also returned to the intimacy of spoken language. In L’Érotisme de vivre, she performed the poetry of Alice Mendelson, accompanied by pianist Grégoire Hetzel under the direction of Mauro Gioia. The scale had changed, but the curiosity remained: another writer, another setting, another way to give words a body. Ringer leaves music full of appetite and contradiction, open to beauty without becoming polite about it. She made eccentricity feel generous, something an audience could participate in. Our thoughts are with her family, friends, collaborators, and everyone who found freedom in her voice. Follow Catherine Ringer: Instagram Facebook Follow Les Rita Mitsouko Instagram YouTube Bandcamp The post Catherine Ringer, the Extraordinary Voice of Les Rita Mitsouko, Has Passed Away at 68 appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Synthpop project TéMèT releases the single “What We Are” on 2 October 2026 on all platforms. The track leans into a Depeche Mode-inspired synthpop sound, more melodic and atmospheric than the project’s previous, darker and more energetic releases. Lyrically, “What We Are” traces a slow unraveling, something rising to the surface that can no longer be hidden, building toward the refrain: “We become what we are.” TéMèT has previously been featured by Side-Line and EBM.gr, and the track “Discord” was included in eLxAr’s Retro Music August compilation. About TéMèT TéMèT is a synthpop and darkwave duo, K1 and MYK, based in Strasbourg, France. The project’s name draws on Tem, the ancient Egyptian deity associated with the setting sun and with creation and endings, and its sound mixes a melodic, atmospheric register influenced by acts such as Depeche Mode with the darker, more energetic material in its earlier catalogue. The duo’s single “Discord,” described by its members as sitting between Depeche Mode and OMD, was released in August 2026, covered by Side-Line and EBM.gr, and later included in eLxAr’s Retro Music August compilation. “What We Are” follows as TéMèT’s next single, out 2 October 2026 on all platforms.

items.body: Industrial rock band Engines of Aggression release the single Wargames on September 28, 2026, through Phoenix, Arizona outfit Sonic 9 Entertainment. A private pre-release preview of the track is available now on the band’s official site. “Wargames” follows the 2025 singles “Start a War” and “Nightmare in Pain Town.” Engines of Aggression describe “Wargames” as mixing mechanized industrial rhythms with a hard-rock edge in the vein of Rob Zombie and Static-X. The current lineup is Tripp on vocals, Ríos on guitar, Sterling on bass and Deech on drums. The band’s own materials state that Engines of Aggression headlined the Whisky a Go Go on the mid-1990s Los Angeles club circuit, with Korn and System of a Down opening for them at the time, and that the band shared bills with Danzig and Henry Rollins. About Engines of Aggression Engines of Aggression formed in Los Angeles in the early 1990s around frontman Tripp Holland, who recruited guitarist Rik Schaffer, drummer Craig Dollinger and bassist Douglas Van Dyck. The band released the “Speak” EP in 1993 on Priority Records and the debut album “Inhuman Nature” in 1994, issued by Priority Records in the US and Virgin in Europe. “Inhuman Nature” was produced by Lamar Lowder, mixed and engineered by Brian Jenkens and mastered by Tom Baker. The band built a following on the Sunset Strip club circuit through the mid-1990s before a collapsed record deal and internal conflict ended that run of activity. Engines of Aggression returned in the 2020s, relocating to Phoenix, Arizona under Sonic 9 Entertainment. The band released “The Black E.P.,” originally issued only in Japan, on June 14, 2024, produced by Steve Duda, whose credits include Nine Inch Nails, Deadmau5 and Rob Zombie. The EP’s four tracks are “New Shanghai,” “Let U Down,” “Moto Psycho” and “Go Fanatic.” The comeback continued through 2025 with the singles “Start a War” and “Nightmare in Pain Town,” both produced with longtime collaborator Lamar Lowder. The current lineup comprises Tripp (vocals), Ríos (guitar), Sterling (bass) and Deech (drums). “Wargames,” due September 28, 2026, is the band’s next single following that 2025 run.

items.body: Suzanne Perry, the vocalist of 1990s dream pop duo Love Spirals Downwards, released the three-track EP “There’ll Be No More Promises” on Projekt Records on September 18, 2026. The EP is available as a name-your-price digital release on Bandcamp and through streaming and download platforms, and is described on its release page as dream pop, ethereal and darkwave. Perry recorded the EP with multi-instrumentalist Cris Miller of the solo dream-pop project Silver Screen. The lead and title track, “There’ll Be No More Promises,” is new material; the second track is a re-recording of the Love Spirals Downwards song “Ladonna Dissima,” originally released on the duo’s 1994 debut album “Idylls”; the third is a cover of Danny Elfman’s “Sally’s Song” from “The Nightmare Before Christmas.” Perry describes her songwriting process as “instinctively formed as an escape. I find myself captivated within the experience of honest expressionistic music brought into being from a deep introspective place.” Miller, discussing his approach to the collaboration, says he “pay[s] special attention to detail and pursue[s] a holistic approach: envisioning the entire sound first, allowing free experimentation during the process, knowing the direction of the song will be uncovered.” There’ll Be No More Promises (ep) by Suzanne Perry Perry is scheduled to perform live at Brickbat Mansion in Portland, Oregon, on Saturday, October 24, 2026. About Suzanne Perry Suzanne Perry is the vocalist of Love Spirals Downwards, the dream pop duo she formed with guitarist and producer Ryan Lum in Orange County, California, in the early 1990s. The project released its debut album, “Idylls,” in 1994, followed by “Flux” (1995), “Ardor” (1996) and “Ever” (1999), largely on Projekt Records, building a reputation within the American dream pop and ethereal scenes alongside labels including Projekt Records. Love Spirals Downwards has been inactive as a group for extended periods since, with Perry periodically re-emerging with new recordings. “There’ll Be No More Promises,” released September 18, 2026, reunites Perry with Projekt Records and pairs her with Cris Miller of Silver Screen. Alongside the new title track, the EP revisits Love Spirals Downwards’ own catalogue with a redesigned version of “Ladonna Dissima” and adds a cover of “Sally’s Song,” continuing the ethereal, harmony-driven sound Perry first established three decades ago.

items.body: During Side-Line’s own AI-assisted research today, September 16, 2026, an AI web-search tool returned a fabricated claim: that Depeche Mode was releasing a new studio album titled “Come This Madness” on September 25, 2026. No such album exists, of course. It was another AI agent — one we developed to check the claims made by other AI tools — that prevented the article from landing in our editorial flow for further work. Since many of you reading this work with AI professionally, we just wanted to give you a technical account of how that specific kind of error happens. It also shows why all publications need to invest in verification when working with AI. And as an extra, here’s a very suitable Depeche Mode video to go along with this article :). The tool searches, then writes a very short summary for us to work on The AI search tool in question does not work like a traditional search engine that returns a ranked list of links. It runs a query, retrieves a set of web pages or snippets that match it, and then uses a large language model to generate a written summary of what those results say. This two-step process, retrieval followed by generation, is standard for AI-assisted search and is usually described as retrieval-augmented generation. The retrieval step worked correctly in this case. The underlying search returned real, relevant results, including a legitimate Mojo magazine feature on Depeche Mode’s Berlin period and coverage of the band’s 40th-anniversary “Black Celebration” material. The failure happened in the second step, when the language model converted those results into prose. Why a language model can state a false fact with confidence Here it gets interesting, of course. A large language model generates text one token at a time by predicting the statistically likely continuation of the text so far, based on patterns learned from its training data. When it is asked to summarize search results, in this case on Depeche Mode, it is not running a database query that returns exact matches; it is composing a new sentence that resembles the kind of sentence that would plausibly follow from the material it has been shown, blended with patterns from unrelated text it saw during training. For a band with a five-decade recording history, dozens of studio albums, tours, and reissues, and a large body of fan and press writing, the model has an enormous internal store of patterns for what a Depeche Mode album announcement looks like: a title, a release date roughly a few weeks out, a label. When the retrieved search results did not contain a clean, direct answer to “Depeche Mode news September 2026,” the model filled the gap with a statistically plausible-sounding invention rather than stating that no such album was found. This behavior is commonly called a hallucination or, more precisely, a confabulation: fluent, well-formed text that is not grounded in any specific retrieved source, generated because the model’s training optimizes for producing plausible continuations, not for flagging uncertainty. No per-sentence source attribution A second technical factor made the error harder to catch at the point of generation. The summary presented several genuine facts, drawn from real search results, alongside the fabricated album claim, in the same paragraph and the same tone, with no inline citation marking which sentence came from which source. When a retrieval-augmented system does not attach a verifiable source link to every individual claim in its output, a fabricated sentence is indistinguishable, on the page, from a verified one. Some AI search tools address this by forcing every sentence to carry a citation and refusing to generate sentences that cannot be tied to a specific retrieved passage; the tool used here did not do that consistently for this query. How the Depeche Mode error was caught Our editorial workflow treats AI-generated claims as unverified until checked against a primary or otherwise reliable source. The AI agent we use for this directly checked official Depeche Mode sources, and none mentioned any album by that title. A separate search of Bing (as a double check for Google) for the same underlying query surfaced no matching result anywhere on the public web, confirming that the claim had no traceable origin. Because it could not be sourced, it was discarded and the Depeche Mode article pitch never ended up in our flow. We found it while routinely checking the results of the AI agents at work to see if the agents were doing their work properly. You have to do this as an AI operator, or you end up with some pretty weird results, as this example shows. Also, you might want to know that we run various AI agents (each specialized in certain data) to catch factual errors in promo copy that we get (you would be surprised how many press texts sent by labels and bands have factual errors) before we start working on the articles themselves.

items.body: Fernando’s Eyes releases the single “Room On Fire” on 25 September via Aenaos Records, the project‘s first new material since last year’s album “Center Of Your World” and its accompanying “Bonus Tracks & Remixes”. A video accompanies the release on the same day. You can pre-save the single right now. Fernando’s Eyes is the solo project of Fernando Honorato, singer and co-founder of Stockholm post-punk band Principe Valiente. “Room On Fire” moves with more directness than the atmospheric material on “Center Of Your World”: Honorato produced the track himself, with co-production and mix by Hans Olsson, layering programmed drums against live toms he played personally. A saxophone part by Swedish jazz musician Lina Langendorf cuts through the arrangement without turning ornamental. Honorato describes “Room On Fire” as a song about leaving without looking back, a deliberate choice rather than a loss, with the production’s forward momentum matching that resolve. About Fernando’s Eyes Fernando Honorato is the lead vocalist and primary songwriter of Principe Valiente, the Swedish post-punk and darkwave band he founded in 2005. In 2025, he opened a more personal creative outlet through the solo project Fernando’s Eyes, starting with the single “A Million Times” and followed by the debut album “Center Of Your World”. “Room On Fire” is the project’s first new single since that album.

items.body: California duo Antania release the single and video “33”, the first taste of their new album The Unholy 33, due 16 October 2026 via Argonauta Records. The digital album follows, with physical CD and vinyl editions to be detailed later. Antania, the project of Doc Luna and Kali Mortem, build “33” entirely without conventional guitars or bass, relying instead on synthesizers, distorted textures and machine-like rhythms. The duo describe their sound as avant-garde black metal filtered through industrial and experimental electronics, citing Dødheimsgard, Mysticum and Thorns alongside the dark electronic legacies of Skinny Puppy and Ministry as reference points. “The Unholy 33” runs eleven tracks: “33”, “DVHM3R”, “Sn0wAnGeL”, “Gloomzday”, “ThUgG33”, “Cykl0pZ”, “Flies”, “AntVniV”, “Frazzledrip”, “Kultz” and “HEarSe”. Following the album’s release, Doc Luna and Kali Mortem head to Asia in support, joining Swedish extreme metal act The Crown for dates in the UAE, Japan and South Korea, followed by an appearance alongside Evergrey in India. About Antania Antania is the Californian duo of Doc Luna and Kali Mortem. The project began as a doom-bass act, releasing the debut album “Lividity” in 2023 before signing with Triad Records later that year. Antania supported Psyclon Nine on a 2024 European tour alongside Devil M. “The Unholy 33” marks the duo’s move to Argonauta Records and a shift toward the avant-garde industrial black metal sound built entirely from electronics.

items.body: Talking Heads’ debut studio album, “Talking Heads: 77,” turns 49 this year. The New York band released the record on 16 September 1977 through Sire Records. Recording took place at Sundragon Studios in New York, with a first block of sessions in April and May 1977 and a final round of overdubs and mixing at ODO Studios in June. “Talking Heads: 77” runs eleven tracks and just under 39 minutes. It was produced by Tony Bongiovi, Lance Quinn and Talking Heads, with Ed Stasium engineering and mixing. All songs were written by David Byrne, except closer “Psycho Killer,” co-written with Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth. The tracklist runs “Uh-Oh, Love Comes to Town,” “New Feeling,” “Tentative Decisions,” “Happy Day,” “Who Is It?,” “No Compassion,” “The Book I Read,” “Don’t Worry About the Government,” “First Week/Last Week…Carefree,” “Psycho Killer” and “Pulled Up.” The cover photograph was shot by Mick Rock, with cover art credited to David Byrne. “Psycho Killer” reached number 92 on the US Billboard Hot 100 after its release as a single in December 1977, and the album itself peaked at number 97 on the Billboard 200 and number 60 on the UK Albums Chart. “Talking Heads: 77” is included in the reference book “1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die” and was ranked among Rolling Stone’s “500 Greatest Albums of All Time.” A remastered deluxe edition followed in 2005 with bonus tracks, and a further expanded box set was released in November 2024 with outtakes and a live 1977 CBGB recording. About Talking Heads Talking Heads formed in New York in 1975 as a trio of David Byrne on guitar and vocals, Chris Frantz on drums and Tina Weymouth on bass, all former students at the Rhode Island School of Design. The three moved into a shared loft on the Lower East Side and began performing at CBGB, the club that anchored the city’s punk and new-wave scene alongside acts such as the Ramones and Television. Jerry Harrison, formerly of the Modern Lovers, joined on guitar and keyboards in 1977, completing the lineup before recording began on the band’s debut album. Sire Records co-founder Seymour Stein signed Talking Heads in November 1976 after seeing the band open for the Ramones. Sessions for “Talking Heads: 77” started at Sundragon Studios in April 1977 with producers Tony Bongiovi and Lance Quinn, with a break in recording for a European tour supporting the Ramones before the group returned to New York in June to finish vocals, overdubs and mixing at ODO Studios. The album was released on 16 September 1977 in the US and UK through Sire, and by Philips Records across continental Europe. Talking Heads followed their debut with “More Songs About Buildings and Food” (1978), “Fear of Music” (1979) and “Remain in Light” (1980), the latter two produced with Brian Eno, before the band’s biggest commercial success with “Speaking in Tongues” (1983) and the concert film “Stop Making Sense” (1984). The band disbanded in 1991. Forty-nine years after its release, “Talking Heads: 77” remains the starting point of that catalogue and the first appearance on record of “Psycho Killer.”

items.body: French covers project Nouvelle Vague will release its Depeche Mode tribute album, A Date with Depeche Mode, on October 30 through Kwaidan Records and [PIAS]. The full 13-track lineup and its guest vocalists are now confirmed, following the March 2027 UK tour of the same name that Side-Line reported in June. The album was recorded between Rio de Janeiro and Paris. It reworks thirteen Depeche Mode songs in Nouvelle Vague’s bossa nova and lounge style, with a rotating cast of guest singers taking one track each. ‘A Date with Depeche Mode’ tracklist “Enjoy the Silence” (feat. Skye Edwards & Larry Love) “Never Let Me Down Again” (feat. Flavia Coelho) “Only When I Lose Myself” (feat. Mélanie Pain) “Shake the Disease” (feat. Fredrika Stahl) “A Question of Lust” (feat. Beth Hirsch) “Behind the Wheel” (feat. Lily Oaks) “Personal Jesus” (feat. Skye Edwards) “Halo” (feat. Phoebe Killdeer) “Leave in Silence” (feat. Nedime Girisken) “Any Second Now” (feat. Morenike) “Just Can’t Get Enough” (feat. Eva de Marce) “Stripped” (feat. Eva de Marce) “Ice Machine” (feat. Lisa Crawley) Skye Edwards, of Morcheeba, and Phoebe Killdeer each sing two tracks. Larry Love, of Alabama 3, joins Edwards on the opening “Enjoy the Silence.” The album ships as an LP (catalog PIASLL244LP) and CD. Three singles have preceded the album. “Enjoy the Silence,” with Edwards and Love, arrived first, with an official video released on Nouvelle Vague’s YouTube channel. “Never Let Me Down Again,” with Flavia Coelho, followed, and “Only When I Lose Myself,” featuring Mélanie Pain, came out on August 27. Nouvelle Vague and Depeche Mode have a prior connection: the band’s 2009 album “3” included a version of “Master and Servant” sung by Depeche Mode’s Martin Gore alongside Nouvelle Vague vocalist Mélanie Pain, who returns as a guest on “A Date with Depeche Mode.” The album leads into Nouvelle Vague’s 13-date “A Date With Depeche Mode” UK tour in March 2027, running from Stratford-upon-Avon on March 4 to Edinburgh on March 20. About Nouvelle Vague Nouvelle Vague is a French covers project formed in Paris in 2003 by producers Marc Collin and Olivier Libaux. The name references French New Wave cinema, the new-wave music the band covers, and bossa nova. Collin’s original idea was to record Joy Division’s “Love Will Tear Us Apart” in a bossa nova arrangement; the duo then recorded versions of Depeche Mode’s “Just Can’t Get Enough” and The Clash’s “The Guns of Brixton” and assembled a debut album over roughly eight months. The self-titled debut, “Nouvelle Vague,” was released in 2004 on Peacefrog and reworked songs by XTC, Modern English, Killing Joke, The Clash, Joy Division, Tuxedomoon, The Cure and The Undertones. The second album, “Bande à Part” (2006), reached number 23 in France and number 79 on the UK Albums Chart, with versions of Buzzcocks’ “Ever Fallen in Love,” New Order’s “Blue Monday,” Echo & the Bunnymen’s “The Killing Moon” and Blondie’s “Heart of Glass.” The third album, “3” (2009), brought in guest vocalists associated with the original songs, including Martin Gore, Ian McCulloch of Echo & the Bunnymen, Terry Hall of The Specials and Barry Adamson. “Couleurs sur Paris” (2010) collected French-language remakes with guests including Vanessa Paradis and Cœur de pirate. Marc Collin also released “Hollywood, mon amour” (2008), applying the same reinterpretation method to 1980s film-soundtrack songs. The project is known for a rotating cast of mostly female vocalists, several of whom went on to solo careers, including Camille, Phoebe Killdeer, Mélanie Pain, Nadéah Miranda and Élodie Frégé. After “3” and “Couleurs sur Paris,” the band reduced its activity before returning with the EP “Athol Brose” and the album “I Could Be Happy” in 2016. Olivier Libaux died in 2021, and Collin has continued to lead the project live. “A Date with Depeche Mode” is Nouvelle Vague’s first album built entirely around a single artist’s catalogue, and its October 30 release now gives a full shape to the tour Side-Line covered in June.
